prize_parts.citation: For the realisation, and the theoretical proposal, of quantum simulation of strongly correlated many-body matter with ultracold atoms in optical lattices

statement.case_for: I keep B001 as a single-part prize with Bloch, Greiner and Zoller. After the full first-round exchange the scientific case has not changed: the superfluid to Mott insulator transition, fermionic Hubbard physics and single-site quantum gas microscopy turned the Hubbard model into a tunable laboratory system, and more than twenty years of independent replication make the interpretation stable. This is the one shortlisted field in which no member disputes maturity, and it is named as a preference or alternative by most of the committee. The chair asked whether the prize should be experimental or mixed. My answer is mixed, because the lattice proposal is the origin of the programme and the experiments are its demonstration, and a citation that names both the realisation and the proposal says what actually happened in the field. The Cirac-Zoller overlap is then handled simply: B001 takes Zoller for the lattice-simulation proposal, and B011 should not be rewarded separately with the same people. Jaksch and Hansch belong in the background material as the origin of the Hubbard-lattice proposal and the early lattice experiments. My configuration is unchanged from round 1, but I hold it more firmly because each competing case has a structural problem that B001 has to a lesser degree: B020 has an unresolved four-for-three credit across two collaborations, B041 has an unsettled mechanism and omitted experimentalists, and B013 has the cleanest credit but the narrowest reach.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains attribution. Five credited names must become three, so Esslinger, whose fermionic Hubbard experiments are a core part of the achievement, and Cirac are left out, and Jaksch is not on the credited list at all. Mehlig is right that the experiment-only trio is the cleaner prize; a mixed trio is more contestable because one theorist sits beside two experimentalists, and Bloch and Greiner then stand for a larger community that includes Esslinger. Lindroth and Mehlig are also right that analogue simulation has so far demonstrated capability on known models more than it has answered an open question such as high-temperature superconductivity, so part of the promise is prospective. There is overlap with the 2001 BEC prize, and I should not hide that I moved from B011 to B001 in round 1 and could be accused of choosing the trio that fits my earlier view. The clock case B013 has a cleaner credit, and if the committee decided that attribution clarity outranks breadth I could support it.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers the experimental trio Bloch, Greiner and Esslinger, keeping Zoller and Cirac out of B001, and says the experiments, not the proposal, established the field.
responses.response: We agree on Bloch and Greiner and on the maturity, and I accept that the experiment-only trio is easier to defend on the narrow question of who did the experiments. Where I disagree is on what the citation should say. Without a theory credit the lattice becomes a platform that happened to exist, and the proposal that made it a quantum simulator drops out of the record. Esslinger's fermionic Hubbard work is a real loss in my version and I do not minimise it. I would accept your trio if the committee prefers a purely experimental prize, and in that case it must be clear that B011 is not prized with Zoller and Cirac in a later year for the same proposal.

responses.point: Lindroth keeps the clocks first, argues that the Katori and Ye credit maps directly onto the idea and its realisation, and treats B001 as her second choice if a defensible three-name configuration can be agreed.
responses.response: I think the proposal I made is the three-name configuration you asked for: Bloch and Greiner for the realisation, Zoller for the proposal, with a citation that names both. I accept that the clock credit is cleaner and that this is a real advantage, which is why B013 is my first alternative. I also accept your point that the simulator has not yet answered a decisive open question. But the Mott transition and the microscope were themselves discoveries of new controlled states and probes of matter, not only demonstrations, and they have reached into condensed matter and quantum information far more widely than the clocks have beyond metrology. I weigh breadth of impact above attribution simplicity here, though only modestly.

responses.point: Olsson says the five-to-three cut in B001 looks more arbitrary than the B041 trio, and that an open pairing mechanism is a question of explanation, not of whether the discovery exists.
responses.response: I accept the second point: a discovery can be robust while its explanation is incomplete, and I do not claim that the open pairing mechanism makes B041 a poor discovery. My concern is timing and fairness. The 2018 experiments are eight years old, Cao and Dean sit outside the credit, and waiting costs little for a field that is clearly durable. On your first point, the allocation in B001 is contestable, but the contest is between very strong people on both sides, whereas in B041 the omitted junior experimentalists cannot be added by any three-name cut. I would not call either allocation arbitrary, and I would support B041 later if the committee takes it up once the mechanism is better understood.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, says the committee should settle the theory-experiment split in B001 explicitly rather than by default, and that Zoller's lattice proposal is arguably the intellectual origin of the Mott experiments.
responses.response: I agree, and my proposal is the explicit settlement: a mixed prize in which Zoller is credited for the proposal and Bloch and Greiner for the experiments, with the citation worded to say so. On B020, I share your view that the science is the strongest on the shortlist. I cannot help resolve the choice between Gianotti, Della Negra, Jenni and Virdee, since it is outside my field, but I note that three different trios have been proposed and that the question of a principled rule for choosing the names has not been answered in the round-1 files. Until it is, I cannot put B020 above B001.

responses.point: Kroll says a pending redefinition of the second is evidence of maturity and not a reason to wait, since the clocks already reach 10^-18 in independent laboratories.
responses.response: I withdraw my round-1 timing objection as a reason against B013. You are right that independent laboratories reach 10^-18 and compare their clocks, so the physics does not depend on action by the CGPM. My remaining reservation is about reach: the clock result is a precision-measurement advance whose main consumers are metrology and tests of constants, while lattice simulators change how many-body problems are studied. That is why B013 is my first alternative and not my preference.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a mixed theory-plus-experiment prize for B001, or prefer the experiment-only trio with Esslinger in place of Zoller.
Whether Jaksch's role in the lattice Mott proposal is adequately represented when only Zoller is credited, and how Hansch and Esslinger should appear in the background material.
Whether analogue quantum simulation will be judged to have produced new physics and not only demonstrated capability.
I rely on my recollection of the priority history of the lattice proposals and the first Mott and fermionic Hubbard experiments and have not verified it beyond the supplied evidence.
statement.conflict_note: My profile shows a connection to circuit QED (B008, not in my preferred configuration): I work in that area, direct WACQT at Chalmers and have Chalmers colleagues in superconducting circuits (Delsing, Wilson), and Chalmers hosted researchers linked to the 2025 prize. I would recuse myself from any decision on B008. Olsson has noted that I am a Chalmers colleague and that she did not rely on my view of B008; I agree that is the right handling. No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B001, B011, B013 or the other shortlisted entries, although WACQT is a superconducting-qubit programme and Cirac and Zoller's ion-trap and cold-atom proposals concern competing platforms, which I disclose for transparency.
